title: Handshake-to-first-token lag breakdowns and proxy handoff characterization
body:
Summary:
We instrumented the client-to-first-token path across a variety of network topologies and proxy configurations to identify where the most variable latency sits for streaming inference requests. The focus is the interval from TCP/TLS handshake completion to the first generated token arriving at the client ("first-token"), specifically when a proxy (L7 edge / sidecar) is present. Primary findings: 1) TLS/TCP handshake is small but can be amplified by proxy handoff queues; 2) server-side token generation is generally stable, but client flush/transport interactions (Nagle, HTTP chunking alignment) add 5–40ms tail in common configurations; 3) HTTP/2 flow-control stall events inside proxies produce long, non-linear tails that are not visible in ingress-only telemetry; 4) QUIC reduces handshake amplification but exposes scheduler/flush batching effects on the server.

Motivation and context:
- Many apps report acceptable median latency, but user-perceived responsiveness is hurt by first-token tails.
- Several customer tickets (CON-4021 family) describe long pauses between request accept and initial stream data.
- Our prior work focused on sustained throughput and token-level throughput; this investigation targets the very first-token path which matters for interactive latency.

Testbed and constraints:
- Client: Linux Ubuntu 22.04 VMs (t3.large-equivalent), Go client using net/http and grpc-go (v1.58), and a QUIC client using quic-go.
- Server: inference runtime (local dev build, commit d1f24b6) running a small transformer decoding at 8 tokens/s per stream to exaggerate first-token visibility.
- Proxies: two proxies tested: (A) edge proxy (nginx-like L7, buffering disabled) and (B) sidecar proxy (in-house multiplexer with HTTP/2 -> local socket).
- Network: controlled latency via tc (0/10/25 ms one-way), with 1 Gbps bw, no packet loss for baseline; additional runs with 0.1% loss to expose retransmission effects.
- Measurement fencing: We captured kernel tcp_info timestamps, TLS handshake times, app-level accept-to-write timestamps, and client-side stream receive timestamps. All events are emitted into tracing spans correlated by trace-id.

Methodology:
1) Warmup: 10k short streams (single prompt) to populate caches, KV warm state.
2) Microbench: 5k streams per configuration (protocol / proxy / network) with uniform prompt length.
3) Edge-case runs: artificial jitter and small message batching on the client to create flush misalignment.
4) Instrumentation: patched runtime to emit: tcp_accept, tls_done, request_parse_done, decoder_first_token_ready, server_write_first_byte, proxy_enqueue, proxy_dequeue, client_read_first_byte.
5) Analysis: compute distributions for intervals: handshake->request_parse, parse->decoder_ready, decoder_ready->server_write, server_write->client_first_byte. Look for long tails and high variance contributors.

Workloads tested:
- short-echo: 6 token completion, cold decoder (~2ms prep)
- chat-turn: 40 token generation, slower decode to simulate realistic models
- batching disabled vs batching enabled (batch window 5ms/20ms)

Key results (selected):
- Baseline (no proxy, zero added network latency): median handshake->first-token = 26ms; 95p = 48ms; 99.9p = 120ms. Largest single contributor at tail: client-side read buffering and Nagle alignment in the client lib.
- Edge proxy (A), tc=10ms: median = 36ms (+10ms network); 95p = 82ms; 99.9p = 210ms. Observed proxy_enqueue spikes where a small burst of concurrent streams (20–50) caused the proxy to batch writes for flow-control optimization, delaying first bytes until an internal flush window fired.
- Sidecar proxy (B) with HTTP/2 multiplexing: median = 39ms; 95p = 110ms; 99.9p = 420ms. Root cause: HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE fragmentation within proxy; when a large number of streams concurrently have tiny writes, the proxy applies headroom heuristics and defers sending until perceived headroom is enough.
- QUIC test (no proxy): median = 29ms; 95p = 54ms; 99.9p = 140ms. QUIC reduced handshake amplification but server batching (Go runtime timer coalescing) produced microbursts that affected 95–99 tails.

Observed patterns and root-cause hypotheses:
- Proxy write-coalescing heuristics: Some proxies intentionally batch small writes to reduce syscalls; this shifts cost from cpu/syscall to latency and disproportionately affects first-token when writers produce very small frames.
- Client flush semantics: Many client libs defer flushing small bodies (or let TCP Nagle delay) unless TCP_NODELAY is set. In languages with buffered writers (Go, node), common client-side patterns can add tens of ms unpredictably.
- HTTP/2 flow-control interaction: When proxy aggregates multiple streams, window updates and internal buffering create scheduling spikes unrelated to network RTT; the symptom is a small number of streams seeing large delays while others are unaffected.
- Kernel scheduling and epoll wake coalescing: On overloaded hosts with many epoll events, wake batching increased observable tail. This is visible when CPU load was artificially raised in a follow-up run.
- TLS handshake amplification at proxies: re-negotiation/OCSP checks are rare in our tests but when present cause long delays; not the dominant factor overall.

Telemetry excerpts (representative numbers):
- Example trace-id abc123: tcp_accept=3.1ms, tls_done=7.6ms, parse_done=1.2ms, decoder_ready=8.9ms, server_write=0.7ms, proxy_enqueue=4.6ms, proxy_dequeue=93.2ms, client_first_read=10.0ms => total first-token=129ms.
- Percentile table (sidecar proxy, tc=10ms, short-echo): median=39ms, p90=96ms, p95=110ms, p99=200ms, p99.9=420ms.

Mitigations tried and results:
- Disable proxy write-coalescing heuristics: p99.9 reduced from 420ms -> 80ms. CPU cost increased ~2% in proxy host, syscalls up ~12%.
- Force TCP_NODELAY on client: reduced median by ~6ms and trimmed some 95p mass; negligible effect on p99.9 for proxy-attached runs.
- Aggressive HTTP/2 flow-control tuning (smaller initial windows + immediate WINDOW_UPDATE): reduced p95 by ~20ms but increased proxy CPU by ~6%.
- Server-side jitter mitigation (emit a tiny pre-write ping byte before first token): improved some client libs where read-blocking was the issue; p50 improved by ~3–10ms, but this is a hack and breaks streaming semantics for strict consumers.

Operational implications:
- Customers using sidecar multiplexers are most exposed to extreme first-token tails; recommend triage on a per-deployment basis.
- For hosted API, our edge proxies must avoid heuristics that batch small writes on user-facing streaming paths by default. Consider opt-in batching for throughput-critical routes.
- SDKs should document and, where safe, set TCP_NODELAY or expose flush primitives to application code.

Action items (short-term):
- (#1) Patch edge proxy default to disable write-coalescing for streaming endpoints. Owner: Arjun. Timeline: 2 weeks.
- (#2) Add server-side metric that exposes "proxy_enqueue_time" split by stream to our Console traces. Owner: Maya. Timeline: 1 week.
- (#3) SDK guidance doc: add note about TCP_NODELAY and flush semantics for streaming clients. Owner: Lina. Timeline: 1 sprint.
- (#4) Run a production canary with proxy change on internal dev cluster. Monitor first-token p99.9 and CPU delta. Owner: SRE. Timeline: after #1.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do different HTTP/2 implementations (nghttp2, netty, envoy) compare when under mixed-stream load? We only tested our sidecar and nginx-like proxy; need broader compatibility matrix.
- Can we expose a streaming hint header that instructs proxies to avoid batching for that route? Tradeoffs: header-based opt-in vs global config complexity.
- QUIC adoption: if QUIC reduces handshake amplification, should we push QUIC for streaming customers? Need to quantify server-side timer batching effects at scale.

Notes to self / rough todos:
- Attach and store raw traces (s3://redwood-traces/handshake-first-token/2027-12-05).
- Link to PR with proxy-change: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/622 (contains replay harness).
- Create demo showing p99.9 improvement for sales/CS talking points.

Appendix: quick reproduction steps (minimal):
1) Start local runtime: ./dev/bin/run_inference --model test-small --listen :8081
2) Start sidecar: ./dev/proxy --mode sidecar --mux --no-write-coalesce
3) Client run: go run ./dev/clients/stream-client --proto http2 --addr localhost:8443 --prompt "hi" --count 5000
4) Collect traces: ./dev/tools/collect-traces --trace-prefix abc123 > traces.json

If we want to iterate: prioritize disabling proxy coalescing in edge and run 24h canary. Keep an eye on CPU and syscall budget.

End of notes.
